lead: Energy methods answer the question that stress analysis alone cannot: how far does the structure move? After this unit you can find the deflection of a truss joint or of a point on a beam from the member forces and the bending moment diagram, and you can release the redundant reactions of an indeterminate beam. You also get two bookkeeping methods, three moments and moment distribution, for a beam that runs over several supports.
about: The unit turns stored energy into a tool for finding deflections and redundant forces. It starts with the strain energy of a member under axial, bending and torsion load, then differentiates that energy to get a displacement (Castigliano’s theorem) and restates the same idea as virtual work with a unit load. The method of joints supplies the member forces a truss needs, and least work handles a redundant member. The unit-load integral then finds beam deflections, releases the redundant reaction of an indeterminate beam, and leads to the two classical methods for continuous beams: the three-moment equation and moment distribution. Every chapter ends with a number a designer would report: a deflection in mm, a reaction in kN, a bending moment in kN·m.

chapters.idea: A linearly elastic structure stores energy equal to half the load times the deflection it causes, and that stored energy can be written in closed form for axial, bending and torsion loading.
chapters.depth: Define strain energy U (joules), linear elasticity, and the fact that U = ½ P Δ for a gradually applied load. Derive and use U = P²L/(2AE) for a bar of constant axial force, U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx for bending, and U = T²L/(2GJ) for a circular shaft in torsion. For stepped or multi-segment members, sum the segment values. Define A (area), L (length), E (Young's modulus), I (second moment of area), J (polar second moment of area), G (shear modulus), M (bending moment), T (torque). Show the standard results: cantilever with tip load P gives P²L³/(6EI); simply supported beam with central load P gives P²L³/(96EI). Mention resilience and proof resilience as the same quantity at the yield load. State that shear strain energy is deliberately left out here.

figure.aria: One stored-energy quantity U branching into the three loading modes, each with its own formula and the symbols it needs.

chapters.example: An aluminium alloy strut has length L = 1.2 m, cross-section area A = 250 mm², E = 70 GPa, and carries an axial load P = 20 kN. (a) Find the strain energy stored. (b) A steel cantilever of length 2 m, E = 200 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, carries a tip load of 1 kN; find its strain energy. Answer: (a) U = P²L/(2AE) = (20 000)² × 1.2 / (2 × 250 × 10⁻⁶ × 70 × 10⁹) = 4.8 × 10⁸ / 3.5 × 10⁷ = 13.7 J. (b) U = P²L³/(6EI) = (1000)² × 8 / (6 × 200 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶) = 8 × 10⁶ / 9.6 × 10⁶ = 0.83 J.
chapters.trap: Writing U = PΔ instead of U = ½PΔ, and using the second moment of area I in the torsion formula where the polar moment J belongs.
chapters.prereq: Mechanics of solids: stress, strain, E, G, I, J; Unit 1 for bending moment diagrams of beams.
chapters.leave: Shear strain energy and shear flow energy to Unit 5; buckling energy to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: For a linear elastic body, the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to an applied load gives the displacement at that load in the direction of that load.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so keep it short. State ∂U/∂P = Δ and ∂U/∂M = θ, with P (load), Δ (deflection), M (moment), θ (rotation), U (strain energy). Explain why the slope of the U–P curve is a displacement: U = ½PΔ = P²L/(2AE), so dU/dP = PL/AE = Δ. Give the dummy-load procedure for a point where no load acts: apply a fictitious load Q, differentiate, then set Q = 0 in the answer. Two examples are enough: one cantilever, one stepped member. Mention Castigliano's first theorem (∂U/∂Δ = P) in one line only, and warn that reactions are not applied loads.

figure.aria: The rising strain energy curve of the aluminium strut and the straight tangent drawn at 20 kN, whose slope of 1.37 J per kN is the 1.37 mm deflection.

chapters.example: A steel cantilever 2 m long has E = 200 GPa and I = 8 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. A tip load P = 1 kN acts at the free end. (a) Write U as a function of the tip load P. (b) Use Castigliano's theorem to find the tip deflection. Answer: (a) U = P²L³/(6EI) = P² × 8/(6 × 200 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶) = 8.33 × 10⁻⁷ P² joules, which is 0.83 J at 1 kN. (b) Δ = ∂U/∂P = PL³/(3EI) = 1000 × 8/(3 × 200 × 10⁹ × 8 × 10⁻⁶) = 8000/4.8 × 10⁶ = 1.67 × 10⁻³ m = 1.67 mm, downward.
chapters.trap: Setting the dummy load to zero before differentiating, and differentiating U with respect to a reaction instead of the applied load whose direction defines the deflection wanted.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for the strain energy formula in each loading mode.
chapters.leave: The general virtual work statement to 2.3; redundant forces to 2.6.

chapters.idea: The work done by a unit load travelling through the real deflection equals the internal work done by the internal forces of that unit load travelling through the real deformations.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so keep it short and to trusses. State the principle: 1 · Δ = Σ nNL/AE, where N is the member force due to the real loads, n is the member force due to the unit load applied at the point and in the direction of the deflection wanted, A is the member area, E is Young's modulus, L is the member length, and the sum runs over every member. For a member with several segments, add the segments inside the sum. Keep one sign convention throughout: tension positive. Note that the method is also called virtual work, the unit load method or the Maxwell–Mohr method. Add a table layout: member, L, A, N, n, nNL/A. State that ∫ mM/EI dx is the same recipe for beams, dealt with in 2.5.

figure.title: Unit load method for a truss
figure.aria: Two separate load cases feeding a per-member product, which is summed to give the deflection.

chapters.example: A plane truss has two inclined members meeting at apex C, attached to pin supports A and B on the same level. AB = 2 m, apex height = 1.5 m, so each member is 1.803 m long. Each member has A = 200 mm² and E = 70 GPa. A vertical load of 10 kN acts downward at C. Find the vertical deflection of C. Answer: equilibrium at C gives member force N = 10/(2 × 0.8321) = 6.01 kN compression in each member. A unit load at C gives n = 1/(2 × 0.8321) = 0.601 compression in each. AE = 200 × 10⁻⁶ × 70 × 10⁹ = 1.4 × 10⁷ N. Δ = 2 × (0.601 × 6010 × 1.803)/1.4 × 10⁷ = 13 020/1.4 × 10⁷ = 9.3 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.93 mm, downward.
chapters.trap: Mixing sign conventions, so one member is taken as tension and another as compression in the same load case; and finding n from the unit load plus the real loads instead of from the unit load alone.
chapters.prereq: 2.2 for the derivative idea, and statics for joint equilibrium.
chapters.leave: Beam integrals to 2.5; redundant trusses to 2.6; truss member buckling to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A truss is solved joint by joint when members plus reactions equal twice the joints; when it is more, the extra members are redundant and equilibrium alone cannot find their forces.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so keep it to plane trusses. Define m (members), r (reactions), j (joints) and the count m + r − 2j: zero means determinate, positive means indeterminate to that degree, negative means a mechanism that cannot carry load. Give r = 2 for a pin and r = 1 for a roller. Method of joints: draw each joint, write ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, assume tension positive, begin at a joint with at most two unknowns. Show zero-force members by inspection (two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint). For a redundant truss, state that one compatibility condition per redundant is needed and point to 2.3 and 2.6. Keep to one worked joint-by-joint example plus a short note on how the redundant case starts.

figure.aria: The 4 m span triangular truss drawn as three joints and three members, with the bottom chord in tension and the two rafter members in compression.

chapters.example: A triangular truss has joints A (pin support), B (roller support) 4 m away on the same level, and apex C at 2 m above midspan. A vertical load of 10 kN acts downward at C. Find the degree of indeterminacy and all member forces by the method of joints. Answer: m = 3, r = 3, j = 3, so m + r − 2j = 0, determinate. Reactions by symmetry: Ay = By = 5 kN. Each rafter is 2.828 m long with sin θ = cos θ = 0.7071. Joint A, vertically: 5 + AC × 0.7071 = 0, so AC = −7.07 kN (7.07 kN compression). Horizontally: AB + (−7.07 × 0.7071) = 0, so AB = +5 kN tension. By symmetry BC = 7.07 kN compression. Check at C: 2 × 7.07 × 0.7071 = 10 kN upward, balancing the load.
chapters.trap: Counting a roller as two reactions when finding the degree of indeterminacy, and reading m + r − 2j > 0 as unsolvable instead of as a call for compatibility.
chapters.prereq: Statics: equilibrium of concurrent forces, free body diagrams.
chapters.leave: Deflection of this truss to 2.3; a redundant truss solved by compatibility to 2.6; member buckling to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The same unit-load integral, written as ∫ Mm/(EI) dx along the beam, gives the deflection at any point of a beam.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so keep to one load case and one stepped member. State 1 · Δ = ∫₀^L M m/(EI) dx, where M is the bending moment due to the real loads, m is the bending moment due to a unit load at the point and in the direction of the deflection wanted, E is Young's modulus and I is the second moment of area. A unit moment gives a rotation. Split the integral wherever I changes. Give the check results: cantilever with UDL gives wL⁴/(8EI); cantilever with tip load gives PL³/(3EI); simply supported beam with UDL gives 5wL⁴/(384EI). Recommend a segment table: limits of x, M(x), m(x), ∫Mm dx.

figure.aria: The real bending moment diagram of the cantilever falling as a parabola from 18 kN·m at the fixed end, against the straight unit-load diagram falling from 3 m at the same end.

chapters.example: A steel cantilever is 3 m long and carries a uniformly distributed load w = 4 kN/m over its whole length. E = 200 GPa and I = 12 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. Using the unit load method, find the deflection at the free end. Answer: measuring x from the fixed end, M(x) = w(L − x)²/2 = 2(3 − x)² kN·m, and the unit load at the free end gives m(x) = (3 − x). Then Δ = ∫₀³ [2(3 − x)² × (3 − x) × 10³]/(EI) dx = 2000 × 3⁴/12 /(EI) = 13 500/(200 × 10⁹ × 12 × 10⁻⁶) = 13 500/2.4 × 10⁶ = 5.63 × 10⁻³ m... recomputing as wL⁴/(8EI): 4000 × 81/(8 × 200 × 10⁹ × 12 × 10⁻⁶) = 324 000/1.92 × 10⁷ = 0.0169 m = 16.9 mm, downward.
chapters.trap: Putting the unit load at the wrong point or in the wrong direction, which gives the wrong m; and dropping 1/EI out of the integral for a stepped beam.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 for the unit-load recipe; Unit 1 for bending moment diagrams.
chapters.leave: Unsymmetrical and thin-walled beam deflection to Unit 4; plate deflection to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A redundant reaction is found by removing it, calculating the displacement that the real loads cause at that point, and writing one compatibility equation that the redundant must cancel.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so two examples are enough. Describe the force (flexibility) method: choose the redundant R, form the determinate primary structure, then write Δ_load + R δ₁₁ = 0, where Δ_load is the displacement at the redundant due to the real loads, δ₁₁ is the displacement at the same point due to a unit value of R, and R is the redundant in kN. Point out that Δ_load and δ₁₁ come from 2.5. Work a propped cantilever under UDL and a fixed-fixed beam under UDL; draw the final bending moment diagram and mark the hogging moment at the fixed end. Note that the degree of indeterminacy of a beam equals the number of redundant reactions.

figure.title: Force method for a propped cantilever
figure.aria: The prop removed, the free-end deflection of the cantilever written down, matched against the deflection the prop reaction causes, and solved for the reaction.

chapters.example: A propped cantilever is fixed at A, propped at B, and is 4 m long. A uniformly distributed load w = 6 kN/m acts over the whole span; EI is constant. Find the prop reaction and the fixing moment at A. Answer: remove the prop, so the primary structure is a cantilever. Downward deflection at B due to the UDL is wL⁴/(8EI). Upward deflection at B due to a prop reaction R is RL³/(3EI). Compatibility: wL⁴/(8EI) = RL³/(3EI), so R = 3wL/8 = 3 × 6 × 4/8 = 9 kN upward. Fixing moment: M_A = wL²/2 − RL = 48 − 36 = 12 kN·m hogging, which matches wL²/8.
chapters.trap: Getting the sign of one displacement wrong, and forgetting the δ₁₁ term, that is, forgetting that the redundant also deflects the point where it acts.
chapters.prereq: 2.3 and 2.5 for the two deflections that go into the compatibility equation.
chapters.leave: Multi-span beams to 2.7 and 2.8; frame analysis is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: For a continuous beam, one equation links the three bending moments at three consecutive supports, so a beam over many supports becomes a set of simultaneous equations in the unknown support moments.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so keep to two spans and one three-span case. State M_A L₁ + 2M_B(L₁ + L₂) + M_C L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂), where M_A, M_B, M_C are the bending moments at three consecutive supports, L₁ and L₂ are the two spans, A₁ and A₂ are the areas of the free bending moment diagrams of the two spans treated as simply supported, and x̄₁, x̄₂ are the distances of their centroids from the outer supports A and C. Give the ready substitution for a UDL: the right side becomes −(w₁L₁³ + w₂L₂³)/4, and for a central point load P it becomes −(3P₁L₁² + 3P₂L₂²)/8. Note that a simply supported end has M = 0 and a fixed end has M unknown.

figure.title: Three moments at three supports
figure.aria: Three consecutive supports of the continuous beam with the two span lengths on the links and the hogging moment found at the middle support.

chapters.example: A continuous beam has two spans, AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, with simple supports at A and C and a continuous support at B. A uniformly distributed load w = 10 kN/m acts on both spans. Find the bending moment at B. Answer: M_A = M_C = 0. The free bending moment diagram of a simply supported span under UDL has area A = wL³/12 and centroid at midspan, so 6Ax̄/L = wL³/4. The equation becomes 2M_B(6 + 4) = −(10 × 6³ + 10 × 4³)/4 = −(2160 + 640)/4 = −700, so 20M_B = −700 and M_B = −35 kN·m, hogging.
chapters.trap: Losing the sign, because a hogging moment at an intermediate support is negative when sagging is positive; and taking the centroid distance from the wrong end of the span.
chapters.prereq: 2.6 for the idea of releasing a redundant; Unit 1 for the free bending moment diagrams.
chapters.leave: Settlement of supports and varying EI are outside this unit; the same beam is solved by iteration in 2.8.

chapters.idea: Moment distribution finds the support moments of a continuous beam by unlocking one joint at a time, sharing its unbalanced moment in proportion to member stiffness, and carrying half of the share to the far end.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so two joints are enough. Define stiffness k = 4EI/L when the far end is fixed and k = 3EI/L when the far end is pinned, distribution factor DF = k/Σk at a joint (it sums to 1), fixed end moment (FEM), and carry-over factor ½ for a fixed far end and 0 for a pinned far end. State the sign convention once: clockwise moments on member ends are positive. Set out the table exactly as the examination expects: joint, member, relative stiffness, DF, FEM, balance, carry over, final moment. Run the iteration until the carry-over is small, then check joint equilibrium. Mention the name Hardy Cross method.

figure.title: Moment distribution for the two-span beam
figure.aria: The distribution table showing the two member ends at joint B, their distribution factors 0.40 and 0.60, the fixed end moments, the balancing shares and the final equal and opposite moments of 35 kN·m.

chapters.example: The same beam as before: spans AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, UDL w = 10 kN/m on both, simple supports at A and C, continuous at B. Find the bending moment at B by moment distribution and check it against the three-moment answer. Answer: both far ends are pinned, so k = 3EI/L gives k_BA = 0.5EI and k_BC = 0.75EI, and DF_BA = 0.5/1.25 = 0.40, DF_BC = 0.60. Fixed end moments for a propped cantilever are wL²/8: +45 kN·m at BA and −20 kN·m at BC, unbalanced +25 kN·m. Distribute −25 in the ratio 0.40 : 0.60, giving −10 and −15, with no carry-over because both far ends are pinned. Final: M_BA = +35 kN·m and M_BC = −35 kN·m, so the moment at B is 35 kN·m hogging, the same value as 2.7.
chapters.trap: Distribution factors that do not sum to 1 at a joint, and carrying over to a pinned end or forgetting that a pinned far end halves the stiffness to 3EI/L.
chapters.prereq: 2.6 for compatibility and 2.7 for the same answer by another route; Unit 1 for the fixed end moment values.
chapters.leave: Sway frames and multi-storey frames are outside this unit; support settlement is not covered.
